learn.hook: Some farmers in the north-east burn a patch of forest, farm it for a few years and move on — while a Punjab farmer uses tractors, tube wells and HYV seeds on the same field every year!
points: Primitive subsistence farming is done on small patches with simple tools like the hoe, dao and digging sticks, using family or community labour. It depends on the monsoon and the natural fertility of the soil.

In slash and burn ('shifting') agriculture, farmers clear a patch of forest, grow food crops, and move to a fresh patch when the soil loses fertility. It is called jhumming in the north-eastern states, bewar or dahiya in Madhya Pradesh, podu or penda in Andhra Pradesh, valre or waltre in south-eastern Rajasthan and khil in the Himalayan belt; abroad it is milpa in Mexico and Central America and roca in Brazil.

Intensive subsistence farming is practised where there is high population pressure on land. It is labour-intensive and uses high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation. Land divided among heirs over generations has made many holdings too small to be economical.

Commercial farming uses modern inputs such as high yielding variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides to get higher productivity. The same crop can be commercial in one place and subsistence in another — rice is commercial in Punjab and Haryana but subsistence in Odisha.

Plantation farming grows a single crop on a large area, using capital and migrant labour, and produce is used as raw material in industries. Examples: tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane and banana. Tea is grown in Assam and North Bengal, coffee in Karnataka.

example.q: A tea estate in Assam covers hundreds of hectares, employs many workers and sends its leaves to a factory on the estate. What type of farming is this, and why?
steps: Only one crop (tea) is grown over a large area — a feature of plantations.
It needs a lot of capital and labour.
Its produce is raw material for an industry (tea processing), and it is grown for sale.
example.answer: Plantation farming — a single commercial crop on a large estate linked to processing industry.

learn.reallife: The banana chips and the cup of Assam tea at your breakfast both come from plantation farming.

games.title: Local names of slash and burn farming
Farming types: true or false?
items: In slash and burn farming, farmers move to a new patch when the soil loses fertility.
Nature restores the old patch's fertility over time while farmers shift.
Intensive subsistence farming is practised where population pressure on land is low.
It is practised where there is high population pressure on land.
Commercial farming uses HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers and pesticides.
These modern inputs give higher productivity.
Rice is a commercial crop in Punjab but mostly a subsistence crop in Odisha.
The same crop can be grown for sale in one region and for home use in another.
Plantation farming grows many different crops mixed together on small plots.
Plantations grow a single crop over a large area.
Tea and rubber are examples of plantation crops.
Both are grown on large estates linked to industries.

quiz.q: Which tools are typical of primitive subsistence farming?
quiz.explain: Primitive subsistence farming uses simple tools like the hoe, dao and digging sticks with family labour.
quiz.mistake: Confuses primitive farming with mechanised farming

quiz.q: Slash and burn agriculture is called 'jhumming' in:
quiz.explain: Jhumming is the name used in the north-eastern states; it is bewar or dahiya in Madhya Pradesh and podu or penda in Andhra Pradesh.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the regional names of shifting cultivation

quiz.q: In slash and burn farming, why does the farmer shift to a new patch of land?
options: The soil of the old patch loses its fertility
The old patch gets flooded every year
quiz.explain: Without fertilisers, soil fertility falls after a few years, so farmers clear a fresh patch and let nature restore the old one.
quiz.mistake: Does not understand the link between soil fertility and shifting

quiz.q: Intensive subsistence farming is practised in areas with:
options: Very few people and lots of land
quiz.explain: With many people and little land, farmers use labour and inputs intensively to get the most from small plots.
quiz.mistake: Thinks intensive farming happens where land is plentiful

quiz.q: Which inputs are the main feature of commercial farming?
options: HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides
Only family labour and digging sticks
quiz.explain: Commercial farming uses modern inputs to obtain higher productivity for the market.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up commercial farming with primitive farming

quiz.q: Rice is a commercial crop in Punjab and Haryana, but in Odisha it is mainly a:
quiz.explain: In Odisha most rice is grown for the farmer's own family; in Punjab and Haryana it is grown largely for sale.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a crop always has the same type of farming everywhere

quiz.q: Which of these is a feature of plantation farming?
options: Many crops are grown together on tiny plots
Farmers keep shifting to new forest patches
A single crop is grown on a large area
quiz.explain: Plantations grow one crop on a large estate using capital and migrant labour, linked to industries.
quiz.mistake: Confuses plantation farming with mixed or shifting farming

quiz.q: Tea plantations in India are mainly found in:
quiz.explain: Tea is a major plantation crop of Assam and North Bengal (Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri).
quiz.mistake: Does not connect tea with the hilly, rainy north-east

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do some farmers burn forests and move, while others use tractors and the same field every year?' Explain the types of farming.
teach.praise: Chirp! Primitive, intensive, commercial and plantation — now I know every way to farm!
teach.nudge: Good start! What about farming for sale with HYV seeds, or growing just one crop on a big estate? What are those called?

learn.hook: India has not one but three crop seasons — that is why your mandi has fresh peas in winter and watermelons in summer!
points: India has three main cropping seasons: rabi, kharif and zaid.

Rabi crops are sown in winter (October to December) and harvested in summer (April to June). Examples: wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard. Winter rain from western temperate cyclones helps these crops in the north.
Kharif crops are sown with the onset of the monsoon and harvested in September–October. Examples: paddy (rice), maize, jowar, bajra, tur (arhar), moong, urad, cotton, jute, groundnut and soyabean.
Zaid is a short season in summer between the rabi and kharif seasons. Examples: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops. Sugarcane takes almost a year to grow.
In Assam, West Bengal and Odisha, three crops of paddy are grown in a year: aus, aman and boro.

example.q: A farmer in Haryana harvests wheat in April. Which season's crop is this, and what could he grow on the same field in June–July?
steps: Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in April–June, so it is a rabi crop.
In June–July the monsoon arrives, which is when kharif crops are sown.
So he could sow a kharif crop such as paddy (if irrigated) or bajra.
example.answer: Wheat is a rabi crop; in June–July he can sow a kharif crop like rice or bajra.

learn.reallife: Juicy watermelons and cucumbers piled up at fruit stalls in May are zaid crops, grown in the short summer season.

games.title: Which season does each crop belong to?

quiz.q: Rabi crops are harvested during:
quiz.explain: Rabi crops are sown in October–December and harvested in April–June.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the harvest time of rabi and kharif crops

quiz.q: Which of these is a rabi crop?
quiz.explain: Gram is sown in winter and harvested in summer, so it is a rabi crop. Paddy, jute and bajra are kharif crops.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all pulses or cereals belong to the same season

quiz.q: Kharif crops are sown:
options: Only in the month of March
After the monsoon ends in December
With the onset of the monsoon
quiz.explain: Kharif crops are sown when the monsoon arrives and harvested in September–October.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the kharif season with the rabi season

quiz.q: Which of these is a kharif crop?
quiz.explain: Cotton is sown at the start of the monsoon and is a kharif crop; wheat, mustard and peas are rabi crops.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up kharif and rabi crops

quiz.q: The zaid season comes:
options: In winter, before the rabi season
In summer, between the rabi and kharif seasons
quiz.explain: Zaid is a short summer season between the rabi harvest and the kharif sowing.
quiz.mistake: Does not know where zaid fits in the year

quiz.q: Which crops are typical of the zaid season?
quiz.explain: Watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables and fodder crops are grown in the zaid season.
quiz.mistake: Confuses zaid crops with rabi or kharif crops

quiz.q: Aus, aman and boro are three crops of paddy grown in a year in:
quiz.explain: Assam, West Bengal and Odisha grow three paddy crops a year — aus, aman and boro.
quiz.mistake: Does not recall the states with three paddy crops

quiz.q: What helps rabi crops grow well in north India during winter?
options: Sea breezes from the Bay of Bengal
quiz.explain: Winter rainfall from western temperate cyclones helps rabi crops in the north.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the monsoon helps winter crops

teach.ask: Gappu is mixed up: 'When do farmers grow wheat, rice and watermelon?' Explain the three cropping seasons.
teach.praise: Chirp! Rabi in winter, kharif with the monsoon and zaid in summer — three seasons, lots of food!
teach.nudge: Good! But what about the short summer season between rabi and kharif? And which crops grow in each?

learn.hook: Your plate of rice, roti, bajra bhakri and dal comes from four very different kinds of crops — each with its own favourite weather!
points: Rice is a kharif crop that needs high temperature (above 25°C), high humidity and annual rainfall above 100 cm; in drier areas it grows with irrigation. Canals and tube wells allow rice in Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan.

Wheat is the main rabi food crop of north and north-west India. It needs a cool growing season, bright sunshine at ripening and 50 to 75 cm of rainfall spread over the growing season. Its two main zones are the Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan.

Jowar, bajra and ragi are millets ('coarse grains') with very high nutritional value. Jowar is the third most important food crop by area and production and is mostly rain-fed. Bajra grows well on sandy and shallow black soils. Ragi grows in dry regions and is very rich in iron, calcium and other micro-nutrients.
Maize is used for both food and fodder. It is a kharif crop needing 21°C to 27°C and grows well in old alluvial soil; in Bihar it is also grown in the rabi season.

Pulses such as tur (arhar), urad, moong, masur, peas and gram need little moisture and survive in dry conditions. Being leguminous crops, they help restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air, so they are grown in rotation with other crops.

example.q: A farmer in Madhya Pradesh grows wheat every year and finds his soil becoming less fertile. Which crop could he rotate with wheat to help the soil, and why?
steps: Wheat takes nitrogen out of the soil.
Leguminous pulses like gram or moong have root nodules that fix nitrogen from the air.
Growing pulses in rotation adds nitrogen back, so the soil regains fertility.
example.answer: A leguminous pulse such as gram, because it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and restores soil fertility.

learn.reallife: Ragi dosa and ragi malt are popular in Karnataka because ragi is rich in iron and calcium — a millet that is great for growing teenagers.

quiz.q: What annual rainfall does rice need (without irrigation)?
quiz.explain: Rice grows well with high temperature, high humidity and annual rainfall above 100 cm; in drier areas irrigation is used.
quiz.mistake: Confuses rice's rainfall need with wheat's (50–75 cm)

quiz.q: How is rice grown in Punjab and Haryana, which get less rainfall?
options: With canal irrigation and tube wells
quiz.explain: Canal irrigation and tube wells have made rice cultivation possible in low-rainfall areas like Punjab and Haryana.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rice can grow only in high-rainfall areas

quiz.q: Wheat requires a cool growing season and bright sunshine at the time of:
quiz.explain: Bright sunshine is needed when the wheat grain ripens.
quiz.mistake: Does not know at which stage sunshine matters

quiz.q: Which are the two important wheat-growing zones of India?
options: Ganga-Satluj plains and the black soil region of the Deccan
quiz.explain: Wheat grows mainly in the Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and the black soil region of the Deccan.
quiz.mistake: Picks hot, humid or very dry regions unsuitable for wheat

quiz.q: Which millet is the third most important food crop with respect to area and production?
quiz.explain: Jowar is the third most important food crop by area and production.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the different millets

quiz.q: Ragi is valued because it is very rich in:
quiz.explain: Ragi is very rich in iron, calcium, other micro-nutrients and roughage.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the nutritional value of millets

quiz.q: Maize grows well in temperatures between:
quiz.explain: Maize needs temperatures between 21°C and 27°C and grows well in old alluvial soil.
quiz.mistake: Guesses extreme temperatures

quiz.q: Why are pulses grown in rotation with other crops?
options: They need the most water of all crops
They remove all nutrients from the soil
Being leguminous, they fix nitrogen from the air and restore soil fertility
quiz.explain: Leguminous pulses fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving the soil for the next crop.
quiz.mistake: Does not know why pulses improve soil

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does rice grow in rainy Bengal but wheat in Punjab? And why are pulses good for soil?' Explain the major food crops.
teach.praise: Chirp! Rice loves heat and rain, wheat loves a cool season, millets love dry land, and pulses feed the soil with nitrogen!
teach.nudge: Good! But what climate does each crop need? And what do pulses do for the soil?

learn.hook: Your morning chai, the cotton of your school uniform, the rubber of your eraser and the jute bag at the sabzi market all grow on Indian farms!
points: Sugarcane is a tropical and subtropical crop needing a hot, humid climate (21°C to 27°C) and 75 to 100 cm of rainfall; irrigation is needed where rain is low. It is the main source of sugar, gur (jaggery), khandsari and molasses, and it needs manual labour from sowing to harvesting.
Oilseeds: groundnut is a kharif crop; mustard and linseed are rabi crops; sesamum is kharif in the north and rabi in the south; castor seed is grown as both rabi and kharif.

Tea was introduced in India by the British. It needs a warm, moist, frost-free climate, deep fertile well-drained soil rich in humus, and frequent showers spread through the year; it is labour-intensive. Coffee in India is mainly the Arabica variety, first brought from Yemen and first grown on the Baba Budan Hills; it is grown in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

Rubber is an equatorial crop that also grows in tropical areas under special conditions: rainfall above 200 cm and temperature above 25°C. It is grown in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and the Garo Hills of Meghalaya.

Cotton grows well in the drier parts of the black cotton soil of the Deccan; it needs high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine, and takes 6 to 8 months to mature. Jute, the 'golden fibre', grows on well-drained fertile soils of flood plains renewed every year (West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha, Meghalaya). Horticulture includes famous fruits like Nagpur oranges and the apples of Jammu and Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh.

example.q: Why is jute grown mainly in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta region of West Bengal rather than in Rajasthan?
steps: Jute needs high temperature during its growth.
It needs well-drained, fertile soil of flood plains, which is renewed every year by river floods.
The delta of West Bengal has both; Rajasthan is dry and has no such flood plains.
example.answer: Because jute needs hot weather and fertile flood-plain soil renewed each year, found in West Bengal's delta, not in dry Rajasthan.

learn.reallife: Jute bags that replace plastic carry bags at many shops come from the 'golden fibre' grown in West Bengal and Assam.

quiz.q: Sugarcane needs a temperature of:
quiz.explain: Sugarcane needs a hot and humid climate with temperatures of 21°C to 27°C and 75–100 cm of rainfall.
quiz.mistake: Guesses an extreme temperature

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT obtained from sugarcane?
quiz.explain: Sugarcane gives sugar, gur, khandsari and molasses; linseed oil comes from the linseed oilseed.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the products of sugarcane

quiz.q: Which oilseed is grown as a kharif crop?
quiz.explain: Groundnut is a kharif crop; mustard and linseed are rabi crops; gram is a pulse, not an oilseed.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the seasons of oilseeds

quiz.q: Coffee cultivation in India was first introduced on the:
quiz.explain: The Arabica variety, first brought from Yemen, was first grown on the Baba Budan Hills.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Baba Budan Hills with other hill ranges

quiz.q: Which climate suits tea cultivation?
options: Warm, moist and frost-free climate with frequent showers
Dry climate with only one shower a year
quiz.explain: Tea needs a warm, moist, frost-free climate with frequent, evenly spread showers so that tender leaves keep growing.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tea can grow in dry or frosty areas

quiz.q: Rubber needs rainfall of more than:
quiz.explain: Rubber needs a moist, humid climate with rainfall above 200 cm and temperature above 25°C.
quiz.mistake: Confuses rubber's need with rice's (above 100 cm)

quiz.q: How many frost-free days does cotton need?
quiz.explain: Cotton needs high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without recalling the textbook figure

quiz.q: Which crop is known as the 'golden fibre'?
quiz.explain: Jute is called the golden fibre because of its golden colour and value.
quiz.mistake: Confuses jute with cotton

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know: 'Where do tea, coffee, rubber, cotton and jute grow, and why there?' Explain these crops to him.
teach.praise: Chirp! Tea loves misty hills, cotton loves black soil, jute loves flood plains and rubber loves heavy rain!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you tell me what climate or soil each crop needs, like black soil for cotton?
